---
title: "How Hooks Work"
---

A captain-hook hook is a rule that runs at one moment in Claude Code's loop and returns a verdict. This page explains that lifecycle. You learn when an event fires, how the dispatch pipeline turns it into a verdict, and how that verdict reaches Claude Code.

## A hook firing

You ban `git stash` in three lines:

```python
from captain_hook import block_command

block_command(r"git\s+stash", reason="git stash is not allowed; use jj shelve")
```

When Claude tries to run `git stash pop`, Claude Code pauses the tool call and runs your hooks first. The hook matches the command, returns a deny verdict, and Claude Code skips the call. Claude reads the reason and reaches for `jj shelve` instead.

That is the whole shape of a hook. The rest of this page traces each stage so you can predict what any hook does before you ship it.

## The lifecycle

Claude Code processes a turn in a loop. It reads the prompt, calls a tool, reads the result, then decides whether to continue or stop. Each labeled point in that loop is an event, and a hook registered for that event runs when Claude Code reaches it.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[User submits prompt] -->|UserPromptSubmit| B[Agent processes prompt]
    B --> C{Needs a tool?}
    C -->|Yes| D[PreToolUse]
    D --> E{Hook blocks?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Tool skipped]
    E -->|No| G[Tool executes]
    G --> H{Tool succeeded?}
    H -->|Yes| I[PostToolUse]
    H -->|No| J[PostToolUseFailure]
    I --> C
    J --> C
    F --> C
    C -->|No| K{Agent stopping?}
    K -->|Yes| L[Stop]
    L --> M{Hook blocks stop?}
    M -->|Yes| B
    M -->|No| N[Done]

    B -->|Launches subagent| O[SubagentStart]
    O --> P[Subagent runs]
    P --> Q[SubagentStop]
    Q --> R{Hook blocks stop?}
    R -->|Yes| P
    R -->|No| C

    B -->|Context too large| S[PreCompact]
    S --> T[Context compacted]
    T --> B

    B -.->|System notification| U[Notification]

    style D fill:#f9f,stroke:#333
    style I fill:#9f9,stroke:#333
    style J fill:#f99,stroke:#333
    style L fill:#99f,stroke:#333
    style Q fill:#99f,stroke:#333
    style A fill:#ff9,stroke:#333
    style S fill:#9ff,stroke:#333
    style U fill:#ddd,stroke:#333
```

Three of these events let a hook change the agent's course. `PreToolUse` is the one event where a hook prevents an action, denying the tool so Claude Code skips the call. `Stop` and `SubagentStop` run the loop the other way, forcing the agent to keep going when it tries to finish early. Every other event is advisory. The hook injects a message into Claude's context but cannot block.

Claude Code fires nine events in total. For when each one fires, the event class it carries, and whether it can block, see [the events reference](../reference/events.qmd).

## The dispatch pipeline

One captain-hook process handles every event the same way, in four stages.

1. **Parse the event.** Claude Code writes a JSON payload to stdin. The CLI reads it and builds a typed event object, so a `PreToolUse` payload becomes a `PreToolUseEvent` with accessors like `tool_name` and `command`.
2. **Match conditions.** Each registered hook is checked against the event. The event must be in the hook's event set, every `only_if` condition must pass, and no `skip_if` condition may pass. Hooks whose conditions all hold are matched. Conditions are covered in [the conditions reference](../reference/conditions.qmd).
3. **Execute matching hooks.** Each matched hook produces a verdict. A handler hook runs its function; a declarative hook returns its configured message. The first hook to block or allow wins and short-circuits the rest; warnings from every hook accumulate.
4. **Format the verdict.** The winning verdict is rendered as the JSON envelope Claude Code expects and written to stdout. A block becomes a deny, a warning becomes injected context, and no verdict means an empty response that leaves the action untouched.

The trace below walks one event through all four stages.

## Tracing a blocked `git stash`

Start with the same hook, written in its full declarative form so every part is visible:

```python
from captain_hook import hook, Event, Tool, Command

hook(
    Event.PreToolUse,
    only_if=[Tool("Bash"), Command(r"git\s+stash")],
    message="git stash is not allowed; use jj shelve",
    block=True,
)
```

`block_command` is a primitive that expands to this same call, and the [primitives reference](../reference/primitives.qmd) lists the rest.

### Parse the event

Claude tries to run `git stash pop`. Claude Code pauses the tool call and sends this payload to the hook process on stdin:

```json
{
  "tool_name": "Bash",
  "tool_input": { "command": "git stash pop" },
  "transcript_path": "/tmp/claude/session/transcript.jsonl"
}
```

The CLI parses that JSON into a typed `PreToolUseEvent`:

```python
evt.tool_name  # "Bash"
evt.command    # "git stash pop"
```

### Match conditions

The pipeline checks the hook against the event. `Event.PreToolUse` is in the hook's event set, so the event matches. Then each `only_if` condition runs. `Tool("Bash")` reads `evt.tool_name` and matches, and `Command(r"git\s+stash")` searches `evt.command` and matches. No `skip_if` conditions are registered, so nothing skips the hook. Every condition holds, so this hook is matched.

### Execute matching hooks

This is a declarative hook with no handler function, so it returns its configured message as a blocking verdict:

```python
HookResult(action=Action.block, message="git stash is not allowed; use jj shelve")
```

A block is final, so the pipeline stops checking further hooks and carries this verdict forward.

### Format the verdict

The block becomes the deny envelope for a `PreToolUse` event, written to stdout:

```json
{
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
    "permissionDecision": "deny",
    "permissionDecisionReason": "git stash is not allowed; use jj shelve"
  }
}
```

Claude Code reads `permissionDecision: "deny"` and skips the tool call. Claude sees the reason and adjusts, reaching for `jj shelve`.

::: {.callout-note title="Block versus warn"}
Set `block=False` and the verdict becomes a warning. The envelope swaps `permissionDecision: "deny"` for `additionalContext`, so Claude reads the message as advice and the tool still runs.
:::
